intro: The Carmel Quartet plays the second movement, Allegro molto capriccioso, of Bartók’s String Quartet No. 2, Op. 17. In this movement the second violin repeats D while the viola plays pizzicato.

sections.label: A · Repeated D, plucked viola
sections.mNote: Second violin repeats octaves beneath a closely turning melody.

sections.label: B · Narrow tunes and repeated notes
sections.mNote: Quick repeated rhythms return between the short tunes.

sections.label: C · Middle episodes, high violin, pizzicato cello
sections.mNote: The middle episodes include a high violin and pizzicato cello.

sections.label: A′ · Repeated-note dance theme again
sections.mNote: The four strings play the repeated-note dance rhythms again.

sections.label: Coda · Prestissimo, with mutes
sections.mNote: The fastest passage begins pianissimo, with all four instruments muted.

cues.title: Repeated D octaves, second violin
cues.text: After a short introduction, the second violin repeats D in octaves while the viola plays short pizzicato notes. The melody moves above and below them, decorated with quick ornaments.
cues.evidence: Roger Parker, Gresham College lecture, 4 December 2007, describes the opening tritones, repeated second-violin D octaves, viola pizzicato and ornamented melody: https://www.gresham.ac.uk/watch-now/bartok-quartet-no-2
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Recordings near Biskra, 1913
cues.text: In 1913 Bartók recorded Arab music around Biskra in Algeria. Its repeated rhythms and richly ornamented tunes are drawn on in this movement. The melodies move within a small compass over a hammered accompaniment.
cues.evidence: The 1913 recordings near Biskra are documented by Vera Lampert in Folk Music in Bartók’s Compositions: https://bartok-nepzene.zti.hu/en/introduction/ . Parker discusses the North African connection and the movement’s narrow melodies: https://www.gresham.ac.uk/watch-now/bartok-quartet-no-2

cues.title: Middle episodes, violin and pizzicato cello
cues.text: In the middle episodes of the loose rondo form, a high violin melody plays above plucked cello. Longer phrases interrupt the repeated-note dance, and the violin line stays well above the pizzicato accompaniment.
cues.evidence: Parker describes the lyrical middle episode for high violin and pizzicato cello within the movement’s loose rondo form. This note covers the central group of episodes: https://www.gresham.ac.uk/watch-now/bartok-quartet-no-2
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First performance, Budapest, 1918
cues.text: The Waldbauer–Kerpely Quartet gave the first performance in Budapest on 3 March 1918. Bartók dedicated the score to its four members, Waldbauer, Temesváry, Kornstein and Kerpely.
cues.evidence: Budapest Bartók Archives, chronological catalogue, BB 75: première date, ensemble and dedication: https://zti.hu/en/ba/bartok-compositions/chronology

cues.title: Return of the repeated-note dance
cues.text: The repeated rhythms return and bring the four string parts close together. Short, ornamented tunes play against the repeated-note accompaniment, and the lyrical episode ends.
cues.evidence: Parker describes the movement’s recurring repeated-note dance and contrasting lyrical episodes: https://www.gresham.ac.uk/watch-now/bartok-quartet-no-2. The note uses the established return section.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Final Prestissimo, muted
cues.text: The final Prestissimo begins pianissimo, with all four instruments muted. Bartók marked the tempo at 200 dotted minims a minute.
cues.evidence: Parker discusses the score’s closing Prestissimo, its mute and pianissimo instructions and the metronome marking of dotted minim = 200: https://www.gresham.ac.uk/watch-now/bartok-quartet-no-2
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: High violin over pizzicato cello
transitions.from: B · Narrow tunes and repeated notes
transitions.to: C · Middle episodes, high violin, pizzicato cello
transitions.how: The central episodes break off the repeated-note dance and bring in longer phrases. A violin plays a melody in a high register above pizzicato cello, and the other string parts play less around it. The plucked cello keeps a small, dry pulse under the violin line.
transitions.evidence: Parker describes the lyrical middle episode for high violin and pizzicato cello. The section covers several central episodes: https://www.gresham.ac.uk/watch-now/bartok-quartet-no-2

transitions.title: Return of the repeated rhythms
transitions.from: C · Middle episodes, high violin, pizzicato cello
transitions.how: After the more lyrical episodes, short repeated notes bring back the dance. The narrow, ornamented melodies are again set against a repeated string accompaniment. The long phrases are replaced by the quick bow strokes and sharp accents of the opening.
transitions.evidence: Parker describes the returning dance rhythms within the movement’s loose rondo form: https://www.gresham.ac.uk/watch-now/bartok-quartet-no-2. The established section marks this return.

transitions.title: Mutes on for the Prestissimo
transitions.how: All four players put on mutes for the closing Prestissimo. The tempo increases and the dynamic is pianissimo. The repeated notes and turning figures continue at the lower dynamic. The metronome marking is dotted minim = 200.
transitions.evidence: Parker describes the final Prestissimo, played pianissimo with mutes, and its metronome marking: https://www.gresham.ac.uk/watch-now/bartok-quartet-no-2

composer.born: 25 March 1881, Nagyszentmiklós, Hungary (now Sânnicolau Mare, Romania)
composer.epithet: Composer who saw a future for concert music in village songs and used a phonograph to record how they were sung.
facts: István Thomán, a Liszt pupil, and Hans Koessler; Budapest Academy, 1899–1903
Piano professor in Budapest, 1907–34; folk-music research in Budapest and at Columbia University
Hungarian, Slovak and Romanian villages; Biskra, 1913; Turkey with Adnan Saygun, 1936
Six quartets, three piano concertos, two violin concertos, three stage works and Mikrokosmos
composer.background:
In May 1904 Bartók went to stay with the Fischer family at Gerlicepuszta. He had a piano sent out, practised four hours a day and composed for four or five more. There he heard Lidi Dósa, a young woman from Transylvania in the family’s service, singing to the children in her care, and began writing down her songs. Their Hungarian music differed from the urban entertainment that usually went by that name, and he wanted more of it. Two years later the writer Béla Balázs went collecting with Bartók and recorded in his diary that the frail-looking pianist wore him out: “I was already very tired, but he kept urging and driving me on to collect more!”

Bartók was born in Nagyszentmiklós in 1881, when the town belonged to Hungary; it is now Sânnicolau Mare in Romania. His father, director of an agricultural school, died when he was seven. His mother Paula supported Béla and his sister by teaching, moving between towns before settling in Pozsony, now Bratislava. At the Budapest Academy he studied piano with István Thomán, who had studied with Liszt, and composition with Hans Koessler.
